AlphaZero

AlphaZero joins Lesson 95's tree search to a learned policy and value. The policy tells the search which moves to look at, and the value replaces random rollouts. The search then produces a better policy than the one it started from, and the network is trained to imitate it. The same loop, with no human games, learned chess, shogi and Go.

1. SearchPUCT with 30 simulations, guided by $p$ and $v$
2. Playsample a move from the visit shares $\pi$
3. Learnmove $p$ towards $\pi$ and $v$ towards the result $z$
4. Repeata better $p$ and $v$ make the next search better

Train it

Each press plays 500 self-play games and learns from them, then plays 40 test games against a perfect minimax player (20 as X, 20 as O). Press it several times. Grey: the raw policy alone (play $\arg\max_a p$, no search). Green: policy plus 30-simulation search.

The maths

A network $f_\theta(s) = (\mathbf p, v)$ gives move probabilities $\mathbf p$ and a value $v \in [-1, 1]$ for the player to move. Search selects moves by the PUCT rule:

$$a = \arg\max_a \big[ Q(s, a) + U(s, a) \big]$$ $$U(s, a) = c\, P(s, a) \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1 + N(s, a)}$$

It is Lesson 95's UCT with the network's prior $P(s, a)$ deciding which moves deserve exploration. A new leaf is not rolled out: its value is $v$ from the network. At the root, noise $P = 0.75\,\mathbf p + 0.25\,\boldsymbol\eta$ with $\boldsymbol\eta \sim \mathrm{Dir}(1, \dots, 1)$ (uniform on the probability simplex) keeps self-play from repeating itself. AlphaZero used smaller Dirichlet parameters for games with more moves.

After the simulations, the visit shares $\pi(a) = N(s, a)/\sum_b N(s, b)$ are the search's policy. Each self-play position $s_t$ becomes a training example $(s_t, \pi_t, z_t)$, where $z_t = +1, 0, -1$ is the final result from the view of the player to move. The loss is

$$\ell = (z - v)^2 - \boldsymbol\pi^\top \log \mathbf p + c_2 \lVert\theta\rVert^2$$

The value is regressed on game outcomes (Monte Carlo targets, Lesson 35). The policy is trained by cross-entropy to match the search. For a softmax policy the gradient of $-\boldsymbol\pi^\top \log \mathbf p$ with respect to the logits is $\mathbf p - \boldsymbol\pi$, so a gradient step of size $\alpha$ moves each logit by $\alpha(\pi_a - p_a)$, the rule used in the table above. The value moves by $\alpha(z - v)$.

This is policy iteration (Lesson 32) with search as the improvement step. Search turns $\mathbf p$ into a stronger $\boldsymbol\pi$. Training turns $\boldsymbol\pi$ into the next $\mathbf p$. The chart shows the improvement operator at work: with search the agent usually loses less often than its raw policy, and the gap closes as $\mathbf p$ absorbs what the search found.
